Silicon nanowires (Si NWs) are versatile one-dimensional building blocks for gas and biochemical sensors, MEMS/NEMS
physical transduction platforms, and integrated electronic devices because of their high surface-to-volume ratios and
compatibility with semiconductor processing. A key limitation of conventional top-down fabrication is its reliance on

The fabrication of suspended sub-100 nm Si NWs without furnace-based thermal processing posed a central challenge, as conventional oxidation and LPCVD steps are crucial for sidewall protection but can contribute to residual-stress development and constrain process integration due to their high thermal budgets. This work addressed that challenge by introducing conformal metallic passivation as a furnace-free alternative, enabling reproducible fabrication of single-crystal NWs with line-widths down to 50 nm, aspect ratios up to 100, and scalable array pitches of 5μm. This study addresses that gap by developing a furnace-free route for suspended sub-100 nm Si NW fabrication. Building on the nanoscale protrusion and DRIE-release strategy of earlier SCREAM-derived Si NW work, the present process replaces the oxide/LPCVD-type sidewall-protection step with sacrificial PVD Cr sidewall coating. The Cr coating preserves the nanoscale Si preform linewidth during DRIE release, enabling suspended Si NWs with critical dimensions down to 50 nm, aspect ratios up to 100, and array pitches of 5 µm, while limiting the maximum process temperature to 180 °C. The process is implemented on both bulk Si and SOI substrates; bulk Si is used to validate morphology and process transferability, while SOI enables electrically addressable devices, including two-terminal NWs and a suspended junctionless FET architecture.

Suspended Si NWs with different dimensions and layouts are fabricated to evaluate the repeatability and robustness of the proposed process (Fig. 3). A critical step in the fabrication process is defining the geometry of the nanoscale preform (Fig. 1e). Cross-sectional analysis is therefore performed to characterize this geometry. Focused ion beam (FIB) milling is used to prepare lamellae after carbon filling of the surrounding region to preserve structural integrity. The samples are subsequently analyzed by transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Figure 1j presents a schematic illustration of the preform cross-section after the shallow Si etch, while Fig. 1k shows the corresponding TEM image. The TEM analysis reveals a Si preform with a \( \text{SiO}_2 \) mask retained on the top surface, consistent with the pattern-transfer process.

The low-thermal-budget process avoids furnace-based oxidation or deposition steps that can introduce intrinsic stress in suspended Si NWs. However, residual stress is not directly quantified in the present sub-100 nm NW devices. The absence of visible sagging, buckling, or deformation during SEM inspection is therefore interpreted as evidence of structural integrity after release, rather than as a quantitative measure of stress. Previous studies have shown that intrinsic stress in suspended Si NWs can arise from fabrication and surface effects, including native-oxide formation, and that its quantification requires dedicated Raman, resonant, or calibrated nanomechanical measurements\(^{44,48,65,66}\). Accordingly, quantitative residual-stress characterization of the present sub-100 nm NWs is left for future dedicated mechanical studies.

The fabrication of suspended sub-100 nm Si NWs without furnace-based thermal processing posed a central challenge, as conventional oxidation and LPCVD steps are crucial for sidewall protection but can contribute to residual-stress development and constrain process integration due to their high thermal budgets. This work addressed that challenge by introducing conformal metallic passivation as a furnace-free alternative, enabling reproducible fabrication of single-crystal NWs with line-widths down to 50 nm, aspect ratios up to 100, and scalable array pitches of 5μm. The process is then extended to SOI substrates to realize two-terminal single-NW and NW-array devices, as well as FET architectures, with electrical measurements confirming predictable resistive and transistor responses, and hydrogen sensitivity at sub-10 nW operating power in two-terminal single-NW devices via nominal 2 nm Pd functionalization. By eliminating furnace-based thermal steps, the approach reduces thermal

The fabrication was demonstrated at the chip level using batch-compatible cleanroom processes, including optical lithography, PECVD/PVD deposition, plasma etching, DRIE release, and stripping/cleaning. The process does not require serial NW placement, transfer printing, individual device assembly, or manual manipulation of released nanostructures, supporting its scalability toward R&D and pilot-line fabrication. Statistical analysis is performed on the overall 20 NWs per geometry from 3 chips, using 100 sampling points per NW to estimate LER, thereby confirming dimensional reproducibility across multiple released structures. For SOI-based devices, resistance statistics from repeated measurements on single NWs and NW arrays are used to assess fabrication performance and reproducibility. Wafer-level yield qualification would require extended process-control studies beyond the scope of the present work.
